Background

In the data folder, you will find data about shark incidents in California between 1950-2022. The data are from: State of California- Shark Incident Database.

Load the libraries

library("tidyverse")
library("janitor")

Load the data

Run the following code chunk to import the data. In this chunk, I am removing NA’s.

sharks <- 
  read_csv("data/SharkIncidents_1950_2022_220302.csv", 
           na=c("NA", "N/A", "Unknown", "NOT COUNTED", "", " ")) %>% 
  clean_names()

Questions

  1. Are there any “hotspots” for shark incidents in California? Show the top five counties with the most incidents.
sharks %>%
  filter(!is.na(county)) %>% 
  count(county, name = "total_incidents") %>% 
  arrange(desc(total_incidents)) %>% 
  slice_head(n=5)
## # A tibble: 5 × 2
##   county        total_incidents
##   <chr>                   <int>
## 1 San Diego                  25
## 2 Humboldt                   20
## 3 San Mateo                  19
## 4 Santa Barbara              19
## 5 Marin                      16
  1. Make a plot that shows the total number of incidents per county.
sharks %>%
  filter(!is.na(county)) %>% 
  count(county, name = "total_incidents") %>%              
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(county, total_incidents), y = total_incidents)) +
  geom_col()+
  coord_flip()+
  labs(title = "Total Number of Incidents per County", x="County", y="Number of Incidents")

  1. Are there months of the year when incidents are more likely to occur? Make a plot that shows the total number of incidents by month. Which month has the highest number of incidents?
sharks %>% 
  filter(!is.na(month)) %>%
  count(month, name = "total_incidents") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(month, total_incidents),
             y = total_incidents)) +
  geom_col()+
  labs(title = "Total Incidents by Month",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Number of Incidents")

October has the highest number of total incidents.

  1. Is there a time of day when most attacks occur? Make a plot that shows the total number of incidents by time of day. Which time of day has the highest number of incidents?
sharks %>%
  filter(!is.na(time)) %>%
  filter(time != "early am",
         time != "afternoon") %>%
  separate(time, into = c("hour","minute"), sep = ":") %>%
  count(hour) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Total Shark Incidents By Hour of Day",
    x = "Hour of Day",
    y = "Number of Incidents"
  )

Around 11am is when the number of incidents are the highest.

  1. How do the number and types of injuries compare by county? Make a table that shows the number of injury types by county. Which county has the highest number incidents? (hint: your table should be in wide format)
sharks_wide <- sharks %>% 
  filter(!is.na(county)) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(injury)) %>% 
  filter(injury != "minor*",
         injury != "none*", 
         injury != "major*",
         injury != "fatal*") %>% 
  group_by(county, injury) %>% 
  summarize(total = n()) %>% 
  pivot_wider(names_from = injury,
              values_from = total)
## `summarise()` has grouped output by 'county'. You can override using the
## `.groups` argument.
sharks_wide
## # A tibble: 21 × 5
## # Groups:   county [21]
##    county               minor  none major fatal
##    <chr>                <int> <int> <int> <int>
##  1 Del Norte                2     1    NA    NA
##  2 Humboldt                 2     9     7    NA
##  3 Island - Catalina        1     3    NA    NA
##  4 Island - Farallones     NA    NA     7    NA
##  5 Island - San Miguel      2    NA     2     1
##  6 Island - San Nicolas     1    NA    NA    NA
##  7 Island - Santa Cruz      1     1    NA    NA
##  8 Island - Santa Rosa     NA    NA     1    NA
##  9 Los Angeles              6     2    NA     1
## 10 Marin                    4     3     9    NA
## # ℹ 11 more rows
sharks_new_wide <- sharks_wide %>%
  mutate(
    total_incidents = 
      ifelse(is.na(minor), 0, minor) +
      ifelse(is.na(none), 0, none) +
      ifelse(is.na(major), 0, major) +
      ifelse(is.na(fatal), 0, fatal)
  )
sharks_new_wide %>%
  arrange(desc(total_incidents))
## # A tibble: 21 × 6
## # Groups:   county [21]
##    county          minor  none major fatal total_incidents
##    <chr>           <int> <int> <int> <int>           <dbl>
##  1 San Diego           8     9     4     2              23
##  2 Santa Barbara       6     9     2     2              19
##  3 Humboldt            2     9     7    NA              18
##  4 San Mateo           4    12     1     1              18
##  5 Marin               4     3     9    NA              16
##  6 Monterey            2     3     8     2              15
##  7 Santa Cruz          3     8     3     1              15
##  8 Sonoma              1     6     8    NA              15
##  9 San Luis Obispo     1     7     3     3              14
## 10 Los Angeles         6     2    NA     1               9
## # ℹ 11 more rows

The county with the highest number of incidents is San Diego.

  1. Use the table from #5 to make a plot that shows the total number of incidents by county.
sharks_new_wide %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(county, total_incidents), y = total_incidents)) +
  geom_col()+
  coord_flip()+
  labs(title = "Total Number of Incidents per County", x="County", y="Number of Incidents")

  1. In the data, mode refers to a type of activity. Which activity is associated with the highest number of incidents?
sharks %>% 
  filter(!is.na(mode)) %>% 
  count(mode, sort = TRUE)
## # A tibble: 8 × 2
##   mode                    n
##   <chr>               <int>
## 1 Surfing / Boarding     85
## 2 Freediving             36
## 3 Kayaking / Canoeing    30
## 4 Swimming               22
## 5 Scuba Diving           20
## 6 Hookah Diving          10
## 7 Paddleboarding          7
## 8 Walking in shallow      1

Surfing/Boarding is associated with the highest number of incidents.

  1. Make a plot that compares the number of incidents by activity.
sharks %>%
  filter(!is.na(mode)) %>%
  count(mode, name = "total_incidents") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(mode, total_incidents), y = total_incidents)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Incidents by Activity",
    x = "Activity",
    y = "Number of Incidents"
  )

  1. Which shark species is involved in the highest number of incidents?
sharks %>%
  filter(!is.na(species)) %>%
  count(species, sort = TRUE)
## # A tibble: 11 × 2
##    species          n
##    <chr>        <int>
##  1 White          181
##  2 Hammerhead       3
##  3 Blue             2
##  4 Killer Whale     2
##  5 Leopard          2
##  6 Salmon           2
##  7 Blue*            1
##  8 Mako             1
##  9 Sevengill        1
## 10 Thresher         1
## 11 blue             1

The Great White shark species is involved in the highest number of incidents (181).

  1. Are all incidents involving Great White’s fatal? Make a plot that shows the number and types of incidents for Great White’s only.
sharks %>% 
  filter(species == "White") %>% 
  mutate(injury = ifelse(injury == "none" | injury == "none*", "None", injury)) %>% 
  count(injury, name = "total_incidents") %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=reorder(injury, total_incidents), y = total_incidents))+
  geom_col()+
  coord_flip()+
  labs(
    title = "Great White Shark Incidents by Injury Type",
    x = "Injury Type",
    y = "Number of Incidents"
  )

When looking at the incidents caused by the Great White Shark, most are not fatal and have no injury at all.
